extracted.intended_audience: federal agency officials, policymakers, and system managers responsible for e-rulemaking/public comment platforms (e.g., OMB, GSA, agency docket managers, IT staff)
extracted.subtask_description: Evaluation and guidance for federal public comment systems (e.g., Regulations.gov, FCC ECFS) covering accessibility, security, identity handling, posting practices, and transparency in notice-and-comment rulemaking.

rubrics_metrics.name: Openness and accessibility of comment systems
rubrics_metrics.description: ECFS has been designed to maximize public participation by making the filing, posting, and retrieval of comments as easy, inclusive, and accessible as possible (available 24 hours a day, 7 days a week; accepts short express comments via a text box and longer standard comments in most file formats; automatically posts submissions to the docket).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Benefits: robust public input improves regulatory policy. Tradeoffs: the more open the system, the greater the opportunity for mischief. Agencies should preserve accessibility while considering enhancements that maintain usability (e.g., user guides, docket home pages highlighting deadlines).

rubrics_metrics.name: Focus on substance over the count of comments
rubrics_metrics.description: When reviewing comments, agencies should focus on the contents rather than the number for or against a position; an agency rulemaking is not a public opinion survey, and a filer's identity is generally not critical to analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Substantive, individualized comments that address proposals and raise significant factual, legal, or policy arguments deserve attention. Systems and practices should support locating substantive material rather than elevating volume.

rubrics_metrics.name: System security, integrity, and monitoring
rubrics_metrics.description: Actively monitor the comment system to ensure it is accessible and secure, and that openness does not impede the public's or the agency's ability to use the system for its intended purpose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Operational work includes ensuring sufficient network capacity, improving search capabilities, implementing antivirus screening and quarantining infected files, and preventing system disruptions. Security enhancements should be balanced against accessibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identity information collection and verification policy
rubrics_metrics.description: Regulations.gov and agency-specific comment websites collect some identity information (e.g., name, email) from commenters who choose to provide it and also accept anonymous comments; the APA does not require commenters to disclose identity, nor require agencies to verify identity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agencies may collect identity info but lack an obligation to verify it under the APA. Possible technical measures (CAPTCHA, identity authentication, two-factor verification) are being considered to distinguish bots and validate contactability, but policy decisions about verification and privacy must be made carefully.

rubrics_metrics.name: Handling of duplicate, near-duplicate, and mass-mailing comments
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies vary in how they treat duplicate or near-duplicate comment text with varied identity information; practices include posting all comments, posting a single example and reporting totals, or retaining comments outside the public system.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Inconsistency across and within agencies can mislead users about how many individuals commented. Agencies should develop clear policies to identify mass campaigns and explain how duplicates are posted or aggregated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transparency of posting practices and data limitations
rubrics_metrics.description: Selected agencies do not clearly communicate their practices for posting comments and identity information; Federal websites should disclose data sources and limitations to help public users make informed decisions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clear disclosure of posting rules (how duplicates are displayed, what identity fields are shown, whether some comments are stored offline) helps users avoid incorrect inferences about who submitted comments or how many individuals participated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Internal agency guidance on commenter identity and intake/response procedures
rubrics_metrics.description: Seven of ten audited agencies have some internal guidance relating to commenter identity, but content and level of detail vary; guidance most frequently relates to comment intake or response-to-comment phases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agencies should codify consistent operational guidance for intake, posting, responding, and recordkeeping so staff handle identity-related issues and duplicates predictably.

rubrics_metrics.name: Usability and search functionality for finding substantive comments
rubrics_metrics.description: Support users and staff to search for and review comments via keyword and full-text searches; improved search functionality helps users access comments already submitted and respond to them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Invest in search optimization, docket home pages highlighting deadlines and major filings, and user interface improvements so reviewers can surface substantive materials and screen out irrelevant or abusive content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tools to distinguish human filers from automated/bot submissions
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider technical tools such as CAPTCHA and other authentication mechanisms to distinguish human filers from bots and automated processes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implementing CAPTCHA, rate-limiting, or other bot-detection tools can reduce automated mass submissions but should be evaluated for accessibility and false positives; stakeholder roundtables and cross-agency coordination are advised.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment of comments stored outside the public docket system
rubrics_metrics.description: Some agencies maintain comments outside the public comment system (e.g., email file archives) rather than posting them online.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agencies should disclose when comments are retained outside public databases and explain how such records factor into the rulemaking record to preserve transparency and fair notice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Policy on accepting and posting offensive, copyrighted, or irrelevant material
rubrics_metrics.description: Some agencies, like the FCC historically, have adopted a policy to 'accept and post online all comments it receives, including duplicates and near-duplicates and comments containing copyrighted, profane, and irrelevant material.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While openness supports participation, agencies must weigh risks (abuse, threats, malware). Policies should define thresholds for withholding or quarantining submissions (e.g., harmful attachments) and how those decisions are communicated.

rubrics_metrics.name: File-type screening and malware protections
rubrics_metrics.description: Stop accepting risky file types (e.g., executable files); screen submissions using antivirus tools and quarantine infected files so they are not posted to public dockets.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: FCC stopped accepting executable files in September 2017; infected submissions should be quarantined and not posted. Agencies should publish accepted file types and their screening practices.

rubrics_metrics.name: System capacity, resilience, and availability
rubrics_metrics.description: Ensure sufficient network capacity to prevent system disruptions and make the system available and resilient to support large volumes of comments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Operational investments should prioritize uptime and scalability to handle spikes in submissions without loss of access or data integrity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aggregation vs. individual posting presentation of duplicates
rubrics_metrics.description: Different posting practices (posting a single example of duplicate comments and indicating the total number vs posting every duplicate individually) affect how users interpret comment volume and consensus.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agencies should choose a consistent presentation method and disclose it to users; aggregation with counts may reduce clutter, while individual posting preserves a full visible record—each approach has tradeoffs for usability and transparency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reporting identity theft or fraudulent submissions to law enforcement
rubrics_metrics.description: Most agencies did not report identity theft complaints to law enforcement; only one audited agency reported such complaints, raising the question whether agencies should standardize reporting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agencies should consider policies or thresholds for escalating identity-theft or criminal submissions to appropriate law enforcement while coordinating with legal/privacy requirements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Follow-up on audit recommendations and implementation tracking
rubrics_metrics.description: GAO made recommendations to agencies to more clearly communicate posting policies; agencies generally agreed and GAO tracks implementation (some agencies, e.g., SEC, have completed actions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Establish formal follow-up and tracking processes to ensure agencies implement recommended transparency and posting-policy changes; periodic status updates (e.g., six-month intervals) are useful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balancing openness with security and user-friendliness
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies historically erred on the side of openness to maximize participation but recognize the need to recalibrate that balance to address threats and abuses while keeping platforms user-friendly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policy decisions should be consensus-driven across stakeholders, weighing accessibility, inclusion, record integrity, and security. Convene cross-bureau working groups and external roundtables to design next-generation systems.
